Stage 02

Statutory Formation & Board Resolutions

Competent registry, governing statute, capital lockup rules, and first board resolution template.

Competent corporate registry

Registro Mercantil Central for the name certificate; Provincial Mercantile Registry of the registered office address for inscription of the deed.

Governing statute

Royal Legislative Decree 1/2010 of 2 July approving the consolidated text of the Spanish Capital Companies Act (Ley de Sociedades de Capital); particularly Articles 4.2, 22, 25-37, 58-68 and 209.

Formation / constitutional filings

Public deed of incorporation (escritura de constitución) executed before a Spanish notary and subsequently presented for inscription in the Mercantile Registry.

Incorporation processing time

⚡ 37 business days (SOP sum)

Paid-up Capital & Blocked Account Regime No Capital Lockup Account Required

The minimum paid-up share capital is EUR 3,000, which must be fully subscribed and paid in cash in the constitution deed. The funds are deposited in a segregated Spanish bank account and may be used only after the company is inscribed in the Mercantile Registry.

Funding & unlock path: Fire safety certificate issued by the technically competent body (OCITE) verifying implementation of the municipal fire protection plan; structural load certificate for the building floor and industrial machinery; occupational health and safety registration under Law 31/1995 and Royal Decree 1215/1997 for workplace storage and machinery safety.

Paid-in capital rule: The minimum paid-up share capital is EUR 3,000, which must be fully subscribed and paid in cash in the constitution deed. The funds are deposited in a segregated Spanish bank account and may be used only after the company is inscribed in the Mercantile Registry.

Pro-Forma First Board Resolution Draft
RESOLVED, that the founding quotaholders subscribe fully the EUR 3,000 corporate capital shown in Exhibit A, and that the bank deposit certificate evidencing payment into the segregated escrow account held at the designated credit institution be delivered to the notary prior to execution. RESOLVED, that the registered office is fixed at Calle [Address], Postal Code, Madrid, and shall serve as the legal seat and administrative headquarters for all statutory purposes. RESOLVED, that [Name] is appointed sole administrator (Administrador Único) with the broadest powers under the Capital Companies Act, and is authorised as legal representative before all public registries and authorities. RESOLVED, that the deed be executed, tax registration be obtained, and all necessary municipal and industrial licences be initiated.
Industrial Access / EIA & Civil Defense Approval Mandatory Environmental Clearance

Consejería de Industria of the Autonomous Community (e.g. Consejería de Economía, Industria y Empleo) together with the Municipal City Council (Ayuntamiento) competent for activity licensing.

Category: Licencia de Actividad y Apertura (municipal economic activity licence covering manufacturing, warehousing and storage of non-toxic wooden toys; also known as 'licencia de apertura' or 'licencia ambiental' when environmental assessment is attached).

Stage 03

Tax Identity & Indirect Tax

Tax authority e-portal, entity tax classification elections, VAT thresholds, and 0% export documentation chain.

Tax ID Application Infrastructure

Competent tax authority

Agencia Estatal de Administración Tributaria (AEAT); official portal: https://sede.agenciatributaria.gob.es

E-government filing portal

For a newly incorporated Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada (SL), the incorporator must apply for a provisional NIF (Número de Identificación Fiscal) before the notarial deed by filing Modelo 036 (declaración censal) and supporting parent entity documents with AEAT. After registration with the Registro Mercantil, obtain the definitive NIF by submitting the deed and registration certificate. Foreign non-resident shareholders without Spanish ID must obtain an NIE first and may require a fiscal representative. The company must also register for VAT (IVA) on the same Modelo 036 before commencing operations.

Tax ID type & application path: Entity_Level_Taxation (Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada is a resident capital company taxed under the Impuesto sobre Sociedades at 25% on worldwide income; no pass-through). — For a newly incorporated Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada (SL), the incorporator must apply for a provisional NIF (Número de Identificación Fiscal) before the notarial deed by filing Modelo 036 (declaración censal) and supporting parent entity documents with AEAT. After registration with the Registro Mercantil, obtain the definitive NIF by submitting the deed and registration certificate. Foreign non-resident shareholders without Spanish ID must obtain an NIE first and may require a fiscal representative. The company must also register for VAT (IVA) on the same Modelo 036 before commencing operations.

Default Tax Classification & Elections

Default tax classification

Entity_Level_Taxation (Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada is a resident capital company taxed under the Impuesto sobre Sociedades at 25% on worldwide income; no pass-through).

Available election forms

No check-the-box election exists. Spanish corporate tax law provides for: (i) a reduced 15% corporate income tax rate for new companies in the first tax period with a positive tax base and the immediately following period (Art. 29 Ley 27/2014); (ii) election for the consolidated tax regime (Grupo de Consolidación Fiscal) under Art. 58 et seq. Ley 27/2014, when a 70%+ controlling interest exists; (iii) participation exemption regime (ETVE) for qualifying foreign shareholdings; (iv) patent box and R&D relief; (v) mandatory ATAD hybrid mismatch disallowance, not elective. All elections are made via Modelo 036 or the annual corporate income tax return (Modelo 200).

VAT / GST & 0% Export Zero-Rating

Standard VAT / GST rate

Mandatory registration threshold (Nexus)

Stage 04

Banking & Treasury Architecture

Central-bank FX diagnosis, tier-1 local banks vs offshore digital EMI matrix, and KYC rejection defense guide.

Foreign Exchange Regime & Central Bank Policy

Current-account convertibility

Spain uses the euro and operates within the EU single market and the euro-area framework. Current-account transactions, including payments for imports, exports, services, royalties, dividends, interest, and ordinary operating expenses, are generally freely convertible and transferable without a general requirement to obtain prior foreign-exchange approval. Capital-account transactions are also generally liberalized, subject to EU sanctions, anti-money-laundering controls, foreign-investment screening, statistical reporting, beneficial-owner verification, tax compliance, and any sector-specific restrictions. An Spanish Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada may generally receive foreign equity, shareholder loans, and commercial payments and may remit legally distributable profits, dividends, interest, and liquidation proceeds to non-residents. Profit remittance requires adequate distributable reserves, approval of the annual accounts and distribution by the competent corporate body, compliance with creditor-protection and net-equity rules, documentary evidence of the underlying transaction, and applicable Spanish withholding-tax and treaty analysis. Dividend and interest payments to non-residents may require withholding, reporting, and beneficial-owner documentation, with possible relief under an applicable double-tax treaty or EU directive subject to anti-abuse conditions. Banks may delay or reject transfers lacking a clear business purpose, source-of-funds evidence, tax information, or sanctions-screening clearance.

Export proceeds surrender rules

Spain has no general statutory export-proceeds surrender obligation, no mandatory conversion ratio, and no general deadline requiring an exporter to convert foreign-currency receipts into euros. Export proceeds may normally remain in foreign-currency accounts or be converted at the company's discretion. The company must retain commercial invoices, transport and customs evidence, contracts, payment confirmations, and reconciliation records. Banks and payment providers may request transaction-purpose information and may report cross-border payment data or suspicious activity. Statistical, balance-of-payments, foreign-investment, tax, customs, and anti-money-laundering reporting obligations can apply depending on transaction size, counterparty, instrument, and reporting framework; these reporting obligations do not constitute a currency-conversion requirement.

Central bank supervision: Banco de España (Bank of Spain), as Spain's national central bank within the Eurosystem, together with the European Central Bank for euro monetary policy and applicable prudential supervision. Foreign-exchange, foreign-investment, payment-statistics, and capital-movement matters may also involve the Spanish Ministry of Economy, Trade and Enterprise, the Directorate-General for International Trade and Investment, and the State Tax Administration Agency.

Offshore Digital Bank / EMI Whitelist

Stripe Fit: High

Medium to High for payment collection, card acquiring, SEPA payments, and marketplace settlements, but not as a complete substitute for a Spanish domestic bank. An EU-authorized electronic-money institution or payment institution may provide services in Spain through passporting, a Spanish branch, or permitted cross-border provision, subject to its authorization scope, safeguarding rules, AML controls, customer due diligence, sanctions screening, transaction limits, and platform risk policies. A non-EU offshore digital EMI cannot lawfully provide regulated payment or e-money services to Spanish customers merely by operating online; it generally requires EU authorization, an authorized EU partner, or an applicable local regulatory basis. EMIs generally do not accept deposits and safeguarded balances are not equivalent to bank deposits or covered by the Spanish Deposit Guarantee Scheme. Stripe and Amazon Pay availability, reserves, settlement timing, rolling holds, chargeback exposure, prohibited-goods rules, and account termination rights must be reviewed separately from the company's bank account.

Core KYC Rejection Triggers & Defense Dossier

Non-resident shareholder, director, or ultimate beneficial owner with no Spanish tax identification or inconsistent identity data

Root cause: Non-resident shareholder, director, or ultimate beneficial owner with no Spanish tax identification or inconsistent identity data

Defense evidence: Valid passports or national identity documents; NIE or other applicable tax identifiers; recent residential-address evidence; notarized, apostilled, legalized, and sworn-translated documents where required; completed beneficial-owner declaration; ownership chart; director appointment evidence; and a signed explanation of the Spanish business purpose.
Opaque ownership chain, nominee arrangements, trusts, or inability to identify the natural-person beneficial owner

Root cause: Opaque ownership chain, nominee arrangements, trusts, or inability to identify the natural-person beneficial owner

Defense evidence: Current registry extracts for every corporate shareholder; constitutional documents; shareholder registers; ownership and control chart through each intermediate entity; trust or foundation documents where relevant; beneficial-owner declarations; board resolutions; and independent corporate-service-provider confirmations.
Inbound capital or shareholder funding inconsistent with the company's size, business plan, or stated source of wealth

Root cause: Inbound capital or shareholder funding inconsistent with the company's size, business plan, or stated source of wealth

Defense evidence: Capital increase or shareholder-loan agreement; corporate approvals; investor bank statements; audited or filed financial statements; tax returns; sale or financing documents evidencing source of wealth; wire-transfer confirmations; a funds-flow diagram; and a written treasury memorandum linking each payment to the approved transaction.
Expected cross-border sales involving Amazon, Stripe, Latin America, high-refund channels, or multiple payment processors

Root cause: Expected cross-border sales involving Amazon, Stripe, Latin America, high-refund channels, or multiple payment processors

Defense evidence: Business plan; website and marketplace URLs; supplier and customer contracts; payment-processor agreements; product catalogue; shipping and fulfillment arrangements; expected monthly volumes; countries of operation; refund and chargeback controls; VAT and customs registrations; and documented transaction-monitoring procedures.
Toy manufacturing or sale activity with unclear product-safety, import, or licensing compliance

Root cause: Toy manufacturing or sale activity with unclear product-safety, import, or licensing compliance

Defense evidence: Product specifications; applicable EU toy-safety conformity assessment; CE-marking records where required; technical file; Declaration of Conformity; EN 71 testing and laboratory reports where applicable; supplier due diligence; timber-origin and sustainability records; packaging and labeling controls; product-liability insurance; and customs classification evidence.
Payments involving sanctioned jurisdictions, sanctioned parties, restricted goods, or unusual intermediaries

Root cause: Payments involving sanctioned jurisdictions, sanctioned parties, restricted goods, or unusual intermediaries

Defense evidence: Counterparty identification; sanctions-screening results; end-user and end-use certificates; commercial invoices; transport documents; customs declarations; contract and payment-chain explanation; export-control analysis; screening logs; and legal sign-off for any controlled or elevated-risk transaction.
Frequent cash deposits, personal-account use, unexplained third-party payments, or commingling of company and shareholder funds

Root cause: Frequent cash deposits, personal-account use, unexplained third-party payments, or commingling of company and shareholder funds

Defense evidence: Written treasury policy prohibiting personal-account use; bank reconciliation procedures; approved signatory matrix; invoices and receipts; cash-register records if any; related-party agreements; loan or dividend documentation; and evidence that all company receipts and expenses are routed through corporate accounts.
Tax-residency, VAT, permanent-establishment, or economic-substance uncertainty

Root cause: Tax-residency, VAT, permanent-establishment, or economic-substance uncertainty

Defense evidence: Spanish tax registration; VAT identification; registered-office and operating-location evidence; lease or warehouse agreements; payroll or contractor records; local management evidence; tax-residency certificates where relevant; filing history; and a written analysis of the company's operating model and transfer-pricing position.

Cross-Border Clearing Corridors & Settlement Fit

Route equity contributions and shareholder loans from the investor's account directly to the Spanish SL's corporate account through SEPA Credit Transfer for euro payments or SWIFT international transfer for non-euro payments. Use the beneficiary's exact legal name, Spanish IBAN, BIC where required, registered address, and a payment narrative identifying the transaction as share capital, capital contribution, or shareholder loan. Spain does not operate a universal foreign-exchange purpose-code system for ordinary corporate wires; the bank may nevertheless require an internal purpose classification, supporting documents, and confirmation of source of funds. Before funding, provide the bank with the deed or corporate resolution approving the capital increase, subscription or loan agreement, ownership records, beneficial-owner information, investor identification, and source-of-funds evidence. Reconcile the incoming payment to the company's ledger and retain the bank advice, accounting entry, corporate filings, and any applicable foreign-investment or statistical declarations. Do not route capital through a director's personal account or an unrelated third-party account.Use SEPA Credit Transfer or SEPA Instant Credit Transfer for eligible euro-area and SEPA supplier payments, subject to bank limits and sanctions screening. Use SWIFT MT103 or its ISO 20022 equivalent for non-SEPA or non-euro payments, with complete originator, beneficiary, intermediary-bank, invoice, and purpose information. Use commercial documentary letters of credit, standby letters of credit, documentary collections, or bank guarantees for higher-risk suppliers or jurisdictions, subject to UCP 600, ISP98, URC 522, applicable sanctions, and the issuing bank's credit requirements. Match each payment to an approved purchase order, commercial invoice, contract, customs or transport document where applicable, and three-way accounting reconciliation. For imports into Spain, coordinate payment with customs classification, import VAT, EORI information, Incoterms, product-safety records, and freight documentation. Apply segregation of duties, dual approval, beneficiary-change callbacks, sanctions screening, fraud controls, and payment-limit governance.Deliverable foreign-exchange forwards with an authorized bank or regulated investment firm, used to lock exchange rates for documented forecast or committed receipts and payments. Apply MiFID II suitability or appropriateness requirements where applicable, EMIR reporting and risk-mitigation obligations, collateral terms, confirmation controls, and hedge-accounting documentation.Non-deliverable forwards for currencies with limited convertibility or delivery restrictions, subject to the counterparty's regulatory permissions, local-currency rules, sanctions screening, EMIR obligations, and documented commercial exposure. NDFs are generally unnecessary for ordinary euro-denominated activity and should not be used for speculative trading.Currency swaps and cross-currency interest-rate swaps with an authorized financial counterparty for recurring or material currency and funding exposures. Document the notional amount, maturity, reset dates, collateral, termination events, valuation, accounting treatment, and underlying exposure.Foreign-exchange options or collars may be used for material and documented exposures where the company understands premium, strike, settlement, margin, and potential-obligation risks. Avoid leveraged, barrier, or complex structures unless independently approved by the board and supported by a formal risk policy.Treasury control minimums: board-approved hedging policy; exposure forecast; permitted-counterparty list; transaction-authority matrix; confirmation and independent valuation; collateral monitoring; quarterly effectiveness review; prohibition on speculative positions; and retention of contracts, confirmations, valuations, and accounting records.

E-commerce / gateway settlement fit: Medium to High for payment collection, card acquiring, SEPA payments, and marketplace settlements, but not as a complete substitute for a Spanish domestic bank. An EU-authorized electronic-money institution or payment institution may provide services in Spain through passporting, a Spanish branch, or permitted cross-border provision, subject to its authorization scope, safeguarding rules, AML controls, customer due diligence, sanctions screening, transaction limits, and platform risk policies. A non-EU offshore digital EMI cannot lawfully provide regulated payment or e-money services to Spanish customers merely by operating online; it generally requires EU authorization, an authorized EU partner, or an applicable local regulatory basis. EMIs generally do not accept deposits and safeguarded balances are not equivalent to bank deposits or covered by the Spanish Deposit Guarantee Scheme. Stripe and Amazon Pay availability, reserves, settlement timing, rolling holds, chargeback exposure, prohibited-goods rules, and account termination rights must be reviewed separately from the company's bank account.

Statutory Filing Calendar

Statutory deliverableDeadline window Government feeDelinquency sanctions
Annual Accounts (Cuentas Anuales) – balance sheet, profit and loss account, statement of changes in equity, and explanatory notes, together with audit report where required For calendar-year accounts: prepare by 31 March; approve at the Annual General Meeting by 30 June; deposit with the Mercantile Registry within one month of approval, i.e. generally by 31 July $0 USD Administrative fine of €1,200–€6,000 imposed by the Mercantile Registrar for late filing; closure of the company's registry sheet until accounts are deposited; prolonged non-filing may trigger judicial dissolution if losses reduce equity below one-half of share capital
Corporate Income Tax Return (Impuesto sobre Sociedades, Modelo 200) Within 25 calendar days following the six-month period after the tax year end; for a 31 December year-end, the deadline is 25 July of the following year (or next business day) $0 USD Late-filing surcharge of 20% if filed within 3 months after the deadline, 10% within 6 months, 5% within 12 months, 2.5% within 18 months; statutory late-payment interest runs from the original date; persistent default enables AEAT embargoes on Spanish bank accounts and assets
Annual VAT Summary Return (Resumen Anual de IVA, Modelo 390) From 1 to 30 January immediately following the calendar year $0 USD Late submission fines between €150 and €600 plus a non-filing penalty of up to €2,000; under-declared VAT triggers late-payment interest and may lead to corrective assessments and asset attachment
Annual Third-Party Operations Report (Declaración de Operaciones con Terceros, Modelo 347) Between 1 and 20 February of the year following the reporting period; required only if annual transactions with any third party exceed €3,000 $0 USD Penalty of €150 per missing or erroneous record, with general fines up to €2,000 when mandatory declarations are not submitted; no administrative strike-off consequence
Annual return deadline

For calendar-year accounts: prepare by 31 March; approve at the Annual General Meeting by 30 June; deposit with the Mercantile Registry within one month of approval, i.e. generally by 31 July

Statutory government annual fee

$0 USD

Late filing penalties

Administrative fine of €1,200–€6,000 imposed by the Mercantile Registrar for late filing; closure of the company's registry sheet until accounts are deposited; prolonged non-filing may trigger judicial dissolution if losses reduce equity below one-half of share capital

Strike-off trigger

Mandatory Audit Threshold Mandatory Audit for All Entities

Turnover: A statutory audit is mandatory for an SL of greater scale than the general exemption. The audit is mandatory when, during two consecutive years, the company exceeds at least two of the three thresholds: balance sheet total over €4,000,000; net annual turnover over €8,000,000; average number of employees over 50. Public-interest entities are always audited. Shareholders holding 5% or more of the share capital may also request an audit.

Statutory corporate income tax (CIT)

25% (Impuesto sobre Sociedades, Art. 29.1 Ley 27/2014)

Dividend withholding tax (WHT)

Mandatory Return Breakdown

Deadline: · Frequency:

Within 25 calendar days following the six months after the fiscal year-end (i.e., by 25 July for calendar-year companies; the filing window runs from 1 July to 25 July); Modelo 202/222 prepayments due in April (first 20 days), October (1-20), and December (1-20) for calendar-year taxpayers

Box-by-Box Return Breakdown (non-resident focus)

BoxField Non-resident guidanceTax-evasion pitfall
Modelo 200, Casilla 1 (Identificación) / Cabeza del modelo Taxpayer identification data: NIF, corporate name, tax period start and end dates, activity code (CNAE 3240), and the election of accounts in euros For the Spanish SL (resident taxpayer), supply the permanent establishment registration if any; non-resident representatives must attach Form 036/037 power-of-attorney data and the tax identification of the ultimate beneficial owner Late filing without prior AEAT notice: surcharge of 1% per calendar month of delay (max 20%) plus late-payment interest; late filing within 3/6/12 months after deadline triggers surcharges of 15%/20%/25% (Art. 27 LGT). Failure to file: proportional penalty of 50% of the unpaid amount plus fixed €200 per omitted data item (min €300), or fixed €400 when no amount is owed (Art. 198 LGT). Incomplete or incorrect returns: penalty of 15% of the amount not declared (Art. 191 LGT), graduated up to 150% where unlawful concealment exists. Late prepayment (Modelo 202/222): surcharges of 1% per month (max 20%) plus interest; additionally, AEAT may impose a 2% depreciation adjustment? No—keep simple.
